title: History 101

jokes.text: BOTH: Troy and Abed back from summer
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed's signature synchronized catchphrase routines are an established running gag from previous seasons
jokes.punchline: Opening the season premiere with their choreographed self-announcement reaffirms their duo dynamic immediately and signals continuity to fans
jokes.explanation: Works almost entirely on the strength of fan investment in the Troy/Abed relationship. Opening the episode with this is a warm welcome back that rewards loyal viewers. High character integration and economy — it does its job in four words.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wait, something's different about my bulletin board.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I had exactly 847 thumbtacks on here before summer break, and now there are 846.

jokes.text: Wait a minute. Something's changed. There's 12 additional thumbtacks on that board. They're driving me crazy.
jokes.setup: Someone has changed their appearance over the summer; everyone expects a comment on the obvious physical change
jokes.punchline: Abed notices and is bothered by 12 additional thumbtacks on the bulletin board rather than the person's new look
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed joke — his hypersensitivity to environmental details over social ones is perfectly in character. The specificity of '12 additional thumbtacks' elevates this from a generic 'Abed is oblivious' joke to something genuinely precise and funny. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what's great about hipsters? They're so committed to being different that they all look exactly the same. It's like they got together and said, 'Let's all shop at the same thrift stores, wear the same vintage glasses, and drink the same overpriced coffee.' You've perfectly captured that contradiction — you're individualistic conformity in human form.

jokes.text: No, I meant this. Trying out the hipster look. It's cool, but also not.
jokes.setup: Abed's odd comment about thumbtacks; Troy redirects to his own new appearance
jokes.punchline: 'It's cool, but also not' — a perfectly circular, self-defeating description of hipsterism that somehow nails the concept
jokes.explanation: The self-referential oxymoron perfectly captures hipster culture's paradox. Troy delivering it with earnest sincerity rather than irony makes it work. Good economy — four words do the job.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You're always three years behind on everything, Jeff. You just discovered skinny jeans.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh, that's rich coming from you. You're so behind on trends, you think 'on fleek' is a medical condition.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That doesn't even make sense.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Exactly. Neither does your fashion sense, and yet here we are.

jokes.text: Congratulations, it's me.
jokes.setup: Group is reuniting for the first day of school; there's an expectation of a cheerful greeting
jokes.punchline: Pierce announces his own arrival as if it's a gift to the room, with zero self-awareness
jokes.explanation: Four words that perfectly encapsulate Pierce's narcissism. His complete lack of self-awareness packaged in maximum economy. The phrasing borrows from hospital delivery-room announcements ('it's a boy!') which adds an extra layer of absurdity.

jokes.text: A little late to the hipster party much? / A little much on the 'much' much?
jokes.setup: Jeff mocks Troy's late adoption of the hipster look with 'A little late to the hipster party much?'
jokes.punchline: Troy immediately calls out Jeff's own dated use of the '-much' construction, turning the insult back on Jeff
jokes.explanation: Elegant little verbal ricochet. Jeff sets up with a '90s-era 'much?' usage, Troy instantly weaponizes it back. The structure is tight, the comeback is instantaneous, and the joke works on a linguistic level — both characters are exposed as uncool in quick succession. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm visualizing myself on a TV show, but people keep leaving bad reviews online. 'This character has no depth.' 'The writing is inconsistent.' 'Why does he keep referencing pop culture?'

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm trying to meditate but I keep refreshing the comments section.

jokes.text: Sorry, I'm late. Damn Mexican cleaning woman did a cha-cha on my glasses
jokes.setup: Pierce arrives late; the group expects a mundane excuse
jokes.punchline: Pierce delivers a casually racist, bizarrely specific explanation involving ethnic stereotyping and dancing
jokes.explanation: The joke's comedic premise is Pierce's oblivious racism, which is an established character trait. The specificity of 'cha-cha' is funny in its absurdity. However, this is one of Pierce's lazier offensive moments — the racism here isn't subverted or commented upon, it just lands and moves on. Character-consistent but not especially crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, you're looking lovely today. You know who you remind me of? Annie Lennox. Yeah, that's right, I went there.

jokes.text: Did you envision a babbling brook like I described? / I started with a babbling brook, then layered in elements from our world. I'm sure fans of the brook will complain, but it was limiting.
jokes.setup: Britta asks if Abed used her suggested relaxation technique (imagining a babbling brook)
jokes.punchline: Abed has already expanded the 'brook' into an elaborate internal universe, speaking about it like a TV showrunner dealing with fan criticism of creative changes
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional Community meta-writing. Abed's response functions simultaneously as: (1) a character moment showing his inability to follow simple instructions, (2) a meta-commentary on TV showrunners expanding/complicating source material, and (3) a wink at Community's own fans who might complain about changes. 'I'm sure fans of the brook will complain, but it was limiting' is a genuinely sharp line that works on multiple levels. High originality, structure, and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm going to my happy place.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's a TV show. Starring me.

jokes.text: Okay. Here's the deal, Jessica Biel. The first day of senior year is emotional for everyone so I hereby therapize you to go to your happy place whenever you feel stressed.
jokes.setup: Britta is trying to help Abed manage anxiety using her pop-psychology approach
jokes.punchline: 'I hereby therapize you' — Britta invents a word to perform an act of therapy she's completely unqualified to give, while calling Abed 'Jessica Biel' for no apparent reason
jokes.explanation: Two good jokes packed together: 'therapize' as Britta's pseudo-professional neologism is a solid character joke about her overconfident amateur psychology. 'Jessica Biel' as a random address is a classic Britta non-sequitur. Neither is exceptional alone but they work in combination.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's literally inside his imagination

jokes.text: Britta tells Abed 'I hereby therapize you' — using 'therapize' as a made-up therapeutic directive
jokes.setup: Britta is playing amateur therapist, as is her recurring habit
jokes.punchline: 'Therapize' — a made-up word delivered with total authority — encapsulates Britta's Dunning-Kruger relationship with psychology
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Britta: she invents pseudo-therapeutic jargon and deploys it with zero self-awareness. Strong character integration, economical delivery. Not quite exceptional because Britta's bad-at-therapy shtick is well-established by S4.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm going to graduate, get into a good college, maybe study engineering or business, travel Europe for a summer, and learn to make the perfect omelette.

jokes.text: Abed's Happy Community College Show — the full happy-place sitcom sequence with live studio audience, theme song, and laugh track
jokes.setup: Britta tells Abed to go to his happy place whenever stressed; Abed retreats into his mind
jokes.punchline: Abed's happy place is a 1990s-style multi-cam sitcom complete with live studio audience applause, theme song, and a cheerful alternate version of the study group
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout conceits. For a show that is itself a single-camera comedy, Abed's happy place being an idealized multi-cam sitcom is a layered, earned meta-joke. It says something true about Abed as a character (he finds comfort in TV tropes), about the show's own form-consciousness, and about the anxiety of change that is the episode's theme. The laugh track and theme song production commitment elevates it. This is what Community does better than almost any other show.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Our wishes come true!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: They captured Osama bin Laden.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And Subway has a new sandwich!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Also, your credit score went down.

jokes.text: Abed's Happy Community College Show is filmed before a live audience inside of my head.
jokes.setup: The multi-cam sitcom fantasy plays out; standard multi-cam shows use the 'filmed before a live studio audience' disclaimer
jokes.punchline: Abed adds '...inside of my head' — acknowledging the meta-construct while deadpanning the absurdity
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — six additional words ('inside of my head') transform a TV cliché into a profound statement about Abed's psychology and the show's meta-awareness. It's the ideal button on the happy-place conceit: funny, character-defining, and philosophically rich all at once. The deadpan delivery requirement makes it actor-dependent but writing-first. This is among the best lines in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: So you're saying whoever gets here first gets the class?

jokes.text: I've decided I'm gonna do senioritis this year. You know, just hanging out and blowing off classes, pullin' pranks, not saying my G's.
jokes.setup: Group is excited about being seniors; Jeff announces his plan
jokes.punchline: Jeff's list of senioritis activities ends with the hyper-specific 'not saying my G's' — dropping the -ing suffix — which he is already demonstrating mid-sentence
jokes.explanation: Smart structural joke — Jeff is already performing the thing he's describing ('pullin', not saying my G's') which creates a self-demonstrating punchline. The specificity of 'G's' as a marker of casual speech is funnier than a generic 'being lazy' line.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Well, it's not like we're... I mean, we're not not... it's just that Jeff and I have this thing where we don't have a thing, but not because we don't want to have a thing, but because having a thing would complicate the thing we already have, which is a non-thing that's better than a thing would be, except when it's not.

jokes.text: Ooh. I'll pull some pranks with you. Okay. Or Jeff or whoever. You know, whoever's around, whatever.
jokes.setup: Shirley enthusiastically volunteers to do pranks with Jeff
jokes.punchline: Jeff immediately and transparently walks it back — 'or Jeff or whoever, you know, whoever's around, whatever' — his discomfort with Shirley's earnestness made audible
jokes.explanation: A quick cringe beat. Jeff's bumbling social retreat is funny but not particularly inventive. The trailing 'whatever' is a nice touch of deflation. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: This is my seat. I sit here every class. You can't just take someone's seat.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: I've marked it. With my blood.

jokes.text: Last year, Troy wished we got Bin Laden and the Dorito taco. But Obama got credit for both.
jokes.setup: Troy and Abed do their fountain wish tradition; Jeff skeptically says wishes aren't real
jokes.punchline: Abed presents as evidence of the fountain's power: Bin Laden's death AND the Doritos Locos Taco — presenting them as equivalent achievements — and Obama stealing credit for both
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's genuinely great jokes. The comedic genius is in the false equivalence — placing the Bin Laden raid and the Doritos Locos Taco as parallel achievements of equal weight, delivered with Abed's total earnestness. Then the kicker: Obama stealing credit for 'both.' The joke has perfect structure, originality, and quotability. It could only come from Abed's particular brand of pop-culture obsession meeting sincere logic.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, Dean, I have to say, seeing you in normal clothes is somehow more disturbing than any of your costumes.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: What? Why?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Because now I know this is a choice.

jokes.text: Could you wish for Jeff to be on time? / No. No wasting wishes on impossibilities.
jokes.setup: Shirley asks if they can wish for Jeff to be on time
jokes.punchline: Troy flatly declares it an 'impossibility' — wishing for Jeff's punctuality is as futile as wishing for magic
jokes.explanation: Clean, well-timed character joke. Troy's matter-of-fact delivery of Jeff's tardiness as an immutable law of physics is a good burn. Not groundbreaking but efficiently executed.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Our registration system has been hacked.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We're investigating the breach as we speak.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: It turns out the 'hacking' was just someone counterfeiting registration forms in a supply closet.

jokes.text: Don't you read Garrett's Twitter? He posted a crisis alert about it.
jokes.setup: Jeff is surprisingly early to save seats for the group
jokes.punchline: Jeff, who projects nonchalance, reveals he monitors Garrett's crisis-alert Twitter feed — implying he's more invested in Greendale than he lets on
jokes.explanation: Good character-based joke. The funniest element is Garrett having a dedicated crisis-alert Twitter feed, which is funny on its own as background world-building. Jeff following it is the character reveal.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Welcome to the Hunger Games... I mean, the Hunger Deans!

jokes.text: Oh, you know what, girls? I gave you the old flyer. Instagram for Besties is in Room 44.
jokes.setup: Jeff is trying to hold seats for the study group and needs to clear out unwanted competition
jokes.punchline: Jeff fabricates a fake class 'Instagram for Besties' to redirect girls away from the seats — a cheerful lie delivered with total confidence
jokes.explanation: 'Instagram for Besties' as a plausible-sounding Greendale class is a good world-building joke — Greendale courses are famously absurd, so this fake one fits right in. Jeff's smooth confidence in delivering the lie is the character layer.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We've implemented several security measures for the red balls. Holograms, serial numbers, and as a final anti-counterfeiting measure... my personal teeth marks.

jokes.text: Showing up early, helping others, sending girls away? Could this be a whole new Jeff Winger? / Don't ruin it by approving it.
jokes.setup: Britta notices Jeff behaving altruistically, contrary to his usual self-serving persona
jokes.punchline: Jeff's response — 'Don't ruin it by approving it' — reveals that his motivation for good behavior is at least partly contrarianism; approval from others would undercut his identity
jokes.explanation: One of the sharper Jeff character jokes in the episode. 'Don't ruin it by approving it' is quotable, perfectly in character, and gestures at something genuinely true about Jeff's psychology — his goodness is partly performative, and he'd rather be caught doing it than praised for it. High economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I'm 14 years old, so graduating early would be a medical miracle.

jokes.text: Oh, so that's progressed. / I mean, it's progressed, but it hasn't 'progressed' progressed. / It's progressive.
jokes.setup: Britta and Annie appear to be discussing Jeff and Annie's romantic situation (inferring from context); Troy walks up
jokes.punchline: The word 'progressed' gets stretched through three increasingly technical uses, ending with Troy's deadpan 'It's progressive' — a non-answer that is somehow also an answer
jokes.explanation: A fun riff on how the same word repeated loses and gains meaning. The structure mirrors the Jeff/hipster exchange earlier (joke 4), but slightly weaker because 'progressive' as a button is less satisfying than the -much ricochet.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Okay, so if you're fine, that means you take the first letter of the word, multiply it by the number of letters in the word, and then—

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Troy, no.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: —subtract the vowels, and that's your code!

jokes.text: Hey. You can't just walk in here. I've been pissing in jars for an hour trying to keep this seat.
jokes.setup: Students are competing for seats in the overbooked History of Ice Cream class
jokes.punchline: Leonard reveals his seat-saving strategy: urinating in jars for an hour, implying he could not leave his seat for any reason
jokes.explanation: Leonard's elderly-man-with-no-filter character means this lands as a grotesque comedy of commitment. The jar detail is specific and vivid. The joke earns its shock by being logical within the scenario — his dedication is both disgusting and oddly admirable. Good Leonard deployment.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know, leaving Greendale is like... it's like finishing the last scoop of ice cream. You think it's going to last forever, but then one day you look down and the cone is empty. And you realize that every lick, every single moment of that ice cream, was precious.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: So I'm not saying goodbye. I'm just... finishing my cone.

jokes.text: All right, all right, all right. Simmer dean.
jokes.setup: Dean Pelton enters to address the chaotic overcrowding situation
jokes.punchline: 'Simmer dean' — a pun on 'simmer down' substituting 'dean' for 'down,' self-referentially inserting his own title into the idiom
jokes.explanation: One of the Dean's signature 'dean puns' — a running gag throughout the series. The joke is in the specificity of the construction: 'simmer down' becomes 'simmer dean' and it somehow works phonetically while also being slightly terrible. That tension between clever and groan-worthy is exactly Dean Pelton's register.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know, life is like a journey. We're all just passengers on a ship, sailing through an ocean of uncertainty, hoping to find our way to shore.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: And sometimes, we need to lean on each other, to be there for one another, because that's what truly matters in this world.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Actually, I prepared this speech three weeks ago. I've been waiting for the right moment to use it.

jokes.text: Dean Pelton enters: 'Simmer dean.'
jokes.setup: Britta says 'Simmer down' at Leonard; Dean Pelton arrives and uses the moment to insert himself
jokes.punchline: 'Simmer dean' — replacing 'down' with his own title/name, a terrible pun he delivers with total self-satisfaction
jokes.explanation: Classic Dean Pelton — inserting himself linguistically where he has no business being. The pun is groan-worthy in the best way, and his delivery of terrible wordplay with absolute confidence is perfect character work. Very economical. 'Simmer dean' is exactly the kind of throwaway line Community fans quote.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I'm Leonardo DiCaprio. See, he was in Inception, which was about dreams. Amelia Earhart disappeared, which is like a dream because it's something that never really happened. So I'm Leonardo DiCaprio dressed as a dream of Amelia Earhart.

jokes.text: This can't be good. He's dressed as himself.
jokes.setup: Dean Pelton enters; characters brace for impact
jokes.punchline: Jeff notes the Dean is 'dressed as himself' — implying that the Dean's normal appearance is so outlandish that his standard attire registers as a costume
jokes.explanation: Sharp, economic character joke. The implication that the Dean's normal look is indistinguishable from a costume is a perfect running commentary on Pelton's flamboyance. The phrasing 'dressed as himself' is elegant — it functions as both a compliment and a roast simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm dressed as Amelia Earhart. She disappeared over the Pacific Ocean in 1937, and to this day, no one knows what happened to her.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: That's so sad.

jokes.text: Someone hacked into the supply closet and counterfeited these History of Ice Cream admission cards.
jokes.setup: The Dean announces a hacking crisis
jokes.punchline: The 'hack' was breaking into a supply closet — and the high-value counterfeited item is admission cards for a History of Ice Cream class
jokes.explanation: Classic Greendale world-building absurdism — the gap between the gravity of the Dean's announcement and the trivial stakes is the joke. 'Hacked into the supply closet' is a good deflation of tech-drama clichés.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Our most critical data is stored in Microsoft Paint.

jokes.text: The Hunger Deans.
jokes.setup: The Dean dramatically declares there is 'only one fair way' to solve the overcrowding problem and leads everyone somewhere
jokes.punchline: The reveal: an elaborate Hunger Games-style competition branded 'The Hunger Deans' — another dean pun, this time attached to an absurd pop-culture parody
jokes.explanation: The joke has two layers working simultaneously: the dean-pun wordplay AND the absurd escalation of a community college dean constructing a Hunger Games competition for a history class. The theatricality of the reveal (the Dean laughing 'Ha-ha-ha' after announcing it) is classic Pelton. High character integration because this exact brand of enthusiastic overkill is uniquely Dean Pelton.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Well, you see, there's a chain of business failures. First, the manufacturer went out of business, then the distributor, then the retailer where you bought it. So technically, nobody's around to honor the warranty.

jokes.text: each one has been marked by my distinct bite print
jokes.setup: The Dean explains the rubber balls are impossible to counterfeit
jokes.punchline: His anti-counterfeiting measure is biting each ball — he has a 'distinct bite print' — implying he has bitten so many things that his dental impressions are catalogued
jokes.explanation: Funny because it implies the Dean has thought deeply about bite-print authentication, and that this is not an improvised solution but a prepared one. The term 'bite print' as a forensic parallel to 'fingerprint' is a good coinage. Classic Dean Pelton overpreparation.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Indeed. In-deed. Like, a deed. Inside me. I'm going to be here for three years.

jokes.text: Whatevs. We'll take it next semes. Ter. Semester.
jokes.setup: Annie says they need to take the class; Jeff is casual about postponing
jokes.punchline: Jeff begins abbreviating 'semester' to 'semes' — his senioritis extending even to syllables — then catches himself and finishes the word
jokes.explanation: A callback to Jeff's senioritis announcement — he was dropping G's, now he's dropping whole syllables. The broken delivery ('semes. Ter. Semester.') works visually/aurally and shows the character momentarily committing to the bit before reality intervenes. Well-executed small joke.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We have to repeat three years. Three years. We have to repeat three years. Three years we have to repeat. Repeat three years we have to. Years three repeat we have to. Have to repeat years three we. Three years repeat to have we...

jokes.text: I took some extra classes online and I'm one history credit away from graduating. / Jeff, you're graduating early? / Well, graduating after 30 can't be characterized as early.
jokes.setup: Jeff reveals he might graduate, which surprises the group
jokes.punchline: Annie says 'graduating early' and Jeff deflects: graduating after 30 can't be 'early' — a self-deprecating acknowledgment of his age and the non-traditional nature of his education
jokes.explanation: Jeff's self-awareness about his age is a reliable character note — he's simultaneously embarrassed and defensive about being a 30-something community college student. The phrasing is sharp: 'can't be characterized as early' uses legalistic language (fitting for the former lawyer) to deflect.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, you're doing this just for ice cream?

dialogue.speaker: Competitor
dialogue.line: Yeah, they said winner gets a gift card to Marble Slab.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm losing to a pre-med student whose only motivation is frozen dairy.

jokes.text: When were you gonna tell us? / I was working on a speech. Believe me, it tied in a lot of things. There was a lot of resolutions and epiphanies. It would have gone down a lot better after we had taken the ice cream class together.
jokes.setup: Group confronts Jeff about not telling them about his impending graduation
jokes.punchline: Jeff reveals he was preparing an elaborate speech with 'resolutions and epiphanies' — a wink at his own (and the show's) habit of ending episodes with Jeff's inspirational monologues
jokes.explanation: Good meta-joke about Jeff's tendency to deliver third-act speeches. The show is explicitly calling out its own structure, which Community does well. 'A lot of resolutions and epiphanies' is funny because it's both a character trait and a show formula being acknowledged simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: If we restart, I'm changing majors. I'm thinking about going into... I don't know, something that doesn't require me to think about my future.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Like what?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I don't know. Hospitality? Event planning?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We actually have a new major for that. It's called 'Wife Studies.'

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's... that's not a real major.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: It is now. And it comes with a sexist waiver policy.

jokes.text: F-I-N-E or F-Y-N-E? / We made one of them a code for 'not fine.' / F-Y-N-E. / Okay, he's fine.
jokes.setup: Troy says Abed is 'fine'; Annie wants to verify
jokes.punchline: Troy and Abed have created a coded spelling system where F-Y-N-E means 'not fine' — the precision of the system combined with its inherent confusion is the joke
jokes.explanation: Classic Troy and Abed world-building comedy. The system they've built is both sweet (they care about communicating Abed's emotional state) and absurd (the system is comically over-engineered for simple communication). The payoff — 'F-Y-N-E / Okay, he's fine' — is a satisfying resolution that works because Annie accepts this logic without question.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm in the Dean's office right now. Just sitting here. He doesn't know why I'm here. He keeps asking me questions, but I don't answer them. I just stare. It's the perfect prank because there's nothing he can actually complain about.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Troy, why are you in my office?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: No answer. Just the stare. The beauty of it is the ambiguity. He's going to spend all day wondering what I'm up to, and I'm not up to anything. That's the prank.

jokes.text: New Jeff is gonna win seven red balls. Because he is not gonna take that class unless you guys are with me.
jokes.setup: Jeff grandiosely declares selfless intentions for the group
jokes.punchline: Jeff frames his selfless act in macho terms ('win seven red balls') and immediately reveals the motivation is partly his own desire for a specific graduation scenario — undercutting the nobility
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy — Jeff's self-serving heroics are a reliable beat. 'Win seven red balls' is an inherently funny phrase. Doesn't transcend formula but delivers.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: We should actually do something for the prank.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh, I have a prank on a prank. I'm going to convince Jeff that Abed convinced me to prank him, but really I'm pranking Abed by making him think his prank worked when actually I'm going to swap out all his DVDs with bootleg copies, so when he tries to watch them, they skip at a crucial emotional moment, making him think they're damaged, so he'll buy new ones, but I've already bought the new ones and hidden them in his room so he'll find them and think he's crazy.

jokes.text: Hey, is mine different than yours?
jokes.setup: Jeff makes a speech about not being able to stay at Greendale forever; Abed rejoins the conversation
jokes.punchline: While Jeff and others are having an emotional conversation about the future, Abed is apparently comparing his coin to others' coins — completely disengaged from the emotional register of the scene
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed comedy of non-engagement. While everyone processes an emotional moment, Abed is focused on a trivial concrete detail. Works because the contrast is sharp and the line is so short.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, you did all that just to make me think Troy was dead?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: It was a prank!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's insane! You could've just jumped out and yelled 'Boo!'

jokes.text: Look out below. Coming in for a Ian-dean.
jokes.setup: The Dean arrives dramatically in another context
jokes.punchline: 'Ian-dean' — a pun on 'Ian Fleming' but also a dean-pun, as the Dean inserts 'dean' into the proper name
jokes.explanation: One of the Dean's weaker puns in the episode — 'Ian-dean' as a pun on 'Ian Fleming' requires some work to parse and the connection to his entrance is loose. It's a dean-pun for dean-pun's sake rather than an organically good one.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. A car full of popcorn? That's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Come on, it'll be fun!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: No, it's... it's a mess, it's a fire hazard, it's—

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Actually, hold on. A car full of popcorn? That's amazing. Let's do it right now.

jokes.text: Amelia Earhart? / Close. I am America's sexiest aviator, Leo DiCaprio.
jokes.setup: Dean Pelton arrives in an aviator costume; Jeff guesses who he's supposed to be
jokes.punchline: The Dean corrects Jeff: not Amelia Earhart but 'America's sexiest aviator, Leo DiCaprio' — a category that doesn't exist, assigned to Leonardo DiCaprio because of his role in The Aviator
jokes.explanation: The Dean inventing the category 'America's sexiest aviator' and assigning it to DiCaprio based on a movie role is good absurdist logic. Jeff's guess of 'Amelia Earhart' shows he's learned to expect the unexpected from Pelton. The subsequent 'Amelia Earhart would have been faster' response is a nice beat.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Dean Pelton, you sly dog. I had no idea you were into this kind of thing. These are some serious heels. And they fit you perfectly? That's impressive. Most men couldn't pull off this look, but you're really working it. I respect the confidence.

jokes.text: And just as his character lost his mind so have I lost your student records.
jokes.setup: The Dean has arrived as 'Leo DiCaprio as Howard Hughes in The Aviator'; he's framing the records loss dramatically
jokes.punchline: The connection between The Aviator's themes of madness and the Dean losing student records is so tenuous and self-serving that the analogy is funnier than the event itself
jokes.explanation: Good Dean Pelton logic — using an elaborate pop-culture framing to announce something mundane and catastrophic. The implication that he dressed as a character to thematically prepare everyone for the news is delightfully unhinged.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh, this? Yeah, I may have gotten a little competitive in dodgeball.

jokes.text: our student records are stored on a Microsoft Paint file, which I was assured was future-proof.
jokes.setup: The Dean explains why records were lost
jokes.punchline: Student records were stored in Microsoft Paint — not a database, not even a spreadsheet — and someone assured him this was 'future-proof'
jokes.explanation: One of the best institutional-absurdism jokes in the episode. 'Microsoft Paint' as a records management system is both specific enough to be real (it's not an invented software) and absurd enough to be clearly wrong. 'Which I was assured was future-proof' compounds the joke perfectly — not only is it Paint, someone confidently endorsed it as reliable. The specificity of 'Microsoft Paint' over a generic 'bad software' elevates this significantly.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I wish for world peace.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! You can't just wish for world peace! That's like wishing for more wishes. It's the first rule of wishing!

jokes.text: our extended warranty is not being honored by the restaurant that used to be Circuit City
jokes.setup: The Dean is cataloguing Greendale's technological failures
jokes.punchline: The school's technology warranty is being disputed by a restaurant that now occupies the former Circuit City building — a perfect capsule of American retail decay and institutional dysfunction
jokes.explanation: Sharp cultural observational joke — Circuit City's closure is a touchstone of American retail failure (2008), and the idea that a restaurant now occupies the space and is somehow responsible for honoring the old electronics store's warranties is a genuinely original comic image. It captures something true about how underfunded institutions function.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I wish all wars would end.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa. You can't just wish for all wars to end without thinking through the consequences. What about all the soldiers who are gonna suddenly be out of work? What about the weapons manufacturers? You're gonna crash the global economy!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: It's just a wish, Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: A wish with no safety protocols is how you end up with a monkey's paw situation, Britta.

jokes.text: I think the fairest way to handle this is to have everyone repeat the last three years.
jokes.setup: The Dean has lost all student records; someone expects a reasonable solution
jokes.punchline: The Dean's 'fairest' solution is simply to have everyone redo three years of community college
jokes.explanation: The Dean's solution is characteristically disproportionate — the 'fairest' framing is what sells it, implying he's considered alternatives and this is the most equitable. It also feeds directly into the episode's theme about being stuck at Greendale forever.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: If all wars were fought like this, it would eliminate... escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You'd go from epic to parody to reality TV in like twenty minutes.

jokes.text: In-dean, I am.
jokes.setup: Someone says 'You can't be serious'
jokes.punchline: 'In-dean, I am' — a pun on 'indeed' with 'dean' substituted in
jokes.explanation: A reliable dean-pun that's slightly more elegant than 'Ian-dean.' 'Indeed' maps cleanly onto 'in-dean' and the response fits the exchange perfectly. Part of the Dean's running pun vocabulary.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: You can't just wish for more wishes, Troy! That's not how it works!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Why not? Who decided that?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Everyone! It's a rule. There are rules to wishing.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Says who?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Says... the universe! You can't just go around wishing for more wishes like some kind of wish anarchist!

jokes.text: We're gonna be here forever. / TROY: Forever.
jokes.setup: Characters despair about potentially having to restart three years
jokes.punchline: Troy echoes 'Forever' in what sounds like his despairing voice — but the word 'forever' is loaded for Troy and Abed fans (their 'Troy and Abed in the morning — FOREVER' bit), adding a layer of irony
jokes.explanation: Brief but resonant for fans of the show. Troy saying 'forever' in a despairing context inverts the usual celebratory use. Small, fan-service joke but efficiently executed.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I wish I'd never said that!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Too late. You've been Britta'd.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: That's not even a real thing!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Now you're getting Britta'd squared.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Stop it!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh, you want to un-Britta yourself? That'll cost you a Britta-reversal fee, plus interest. We're talking Britta'd to the power of Britta.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: This is ridiculous!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Ridiculous? That's a Britta-and-a-half right there. You're looking at a full Britta-ectomy at this point.

jokes.text: My first red ball is way up high. / To touch my ball, first touch the sky.
jokes.setup: The Hunger Deans competition begins; Dean announces the first challenge with a rhyming couplet
jokes.punchline: The Dean has written rhyming instructions for his Hunger Games competition, treating a community college dispute over a history class with epic, theatrical ceremony
jokes.explanation: The rhyming couplet format for a rubber ball challenge is a good Dean Pelton touch — he's so committed to the theatrical conceit that he's written verse for it. The gap between the gravity of the poetry and the pettiness of the prize (a rubber ball for ice cream class) is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You know what, Britta? I'm done pretending I don't care about anything!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You actually hurt my feelings, and that's... that's not cool.

jokes.text: Jeff's really going after that ball. There's gotta be a joke in there somewhere.
jokes.setup: Jeff is literally and physically trying to get a red rubber ball
jokes.punchline: Britta acknowledges the double-entendre potential in 'Jeff going after his ball' but resists making it, then immediately implies it anyway by saying 'there's gotta be a joke in there'
jokes.explanation: Smart meta-move: the show acknowledges the double-entendre without making it, which is actually funnier than making it. Britta as the character who notices-but-doesn't-commit is appropriate. The audience gets the joke without the show having to lower itself to making it explicitly.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: Oh yes, I'm so excited about hospital administration. I can already picture myself: middle-aged, divorced, having an affair with a radiologist named Dennis who smells like old coffee and broken dreams. We'll meet in the supply closet every Thursday at 2 PM, and he'll tell me I'm 'different' from his wife. By 2025, I'll be wearing exclusively beige and won't remember what joy feels like.

jokes.text: If we're doing the first three years over again, I could change majors. / I've always been curious about forensics. / Did you know you could major in antics? / You need a tomfoolery prereq. They waive it for women.
jokes.setup: Characters contemplate redoing their college years
jokes.punchline: Pierce claims you can major in 'antics,' requires a 'tomfoolery prereq,' but it's waived for women — escalating nonsense delivered with Pierce's confident misinformation
jokes.explanation: 'Major in antics' and 'tomfoolery prereq' are genuinely funny coinages. The escalation to the sexist-but-backward 'waived for women' is an odd Pierce-specific twist — it's not entirely clear why women get the waiver, and the ambiguity makes it funnier. Good absurdist escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: I can see it now. In five years, I'll have expanded my sandwich business into a full restaurant empire. I'll be on the cover of Black Enterprise magazine. My children will be at Ivy League schools. I'll have a summer home in Martha's Vineyard and winter home in Boca Raton.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That sounds great, Shirley. Hey, what do you think about—

dialogue.speaker: Shirley
dialogue.line: And I'll finally get that kitchen with the double ovens, the marble countertops, the Sub-Zero refrigerator that I've always dreamed of. My husband will have learned to appreciate my culinary genius. Our love will be stronger than ever, forged in the fires of entrepreneurial success and—

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh no. Oh no no no. I opened the Shirley vision box. I can't close it. Why did I ask?

jokes.text: 'That's my first ball. New Jeff.' — Jeff to himself after winning the climbing competition
jokes.setup: Jeff wins the first physical challenge
jokes.punchline: He congratulates himself in the third person with his own branding, confirming that 'New Jeff' is just 'Old Jeff' with better PR
jokes.explanation: Functional running gag payoff on the New Jeff branding. The self-congratulation in the third person is a nice touch. Not among the stronger jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: We're seniors! We're basically already gone. Nothing matters anymore!

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Woop woop! Existential dread!

jokes.text: Hey, there's a freshman mixer tonight. Are you guys freshmen? / We can be.
jokes.setup: Chaos over student records; a student asks if they're freshmen
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'we can be' — immediately embracing the opportunity to reinvent himself as a freshman, undercutting his earlier 'new Jeff' maturity
jokes.explanation: Jeff's 'we can be' is the right amount of resigned opportunism. It captures Jeff's willingness to take whatever advantage is available. Brief but lands.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: I need you to come into my office and help me with something long and hard.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay, what is it?

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: It's a wooden beam I'm trying to—

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm gonna stop you right there.

jokes.text: This prank is amazing. He's gonna come in here later and have the creepy feeling someone was in here.
jokes.setup: Shirley and Pierce have broken into the Dean's office for a prank, but apparently done nothing
jokes.punchline: Shirley describes doing nothing as 'amazing' — the prank is to leave a subtle psychological discomfort without any visible evidence
jokes.explanation: Good subversion of the prank setup — the prank is to do nothing, leaving only psychological unease. Shirley's enthusiasm for this non-action is funny. It's a clever commentary on the anxiety of being watched.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm going with her. She's clearly the best dancer here.

dialogue.speaker: Judge
dialogue.line: I'm judging this competition.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Let's move everything on his desk over an inch except his stapler. Then he'll think we moved his stapler. There's so many levels to this.
jokes.setup: Pierce suggests filling the Dean's car with popcorn; Shirley proposes an alternative prank
jokes.punchline: Moving everything EXCEPT the stapler so he'll focus on the stapler — a prank so subtle and psychological it creates a reality distortion field. 'There's so many levels to this' said earnestly about moving desk items an inch
jokes.explanation: One of the most original jokes in the episode. The logic is impeccable and funny: by moving everything EXCEPT the stapler, the Dean will irrationally fixate on the stapler. Shirley's earnest pride — 'There's so many levels to this' — about what is objectively a minimal prank is perfect character comedy. The idea itself is genuinely clever and the character's investment in it makes it land even harder.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: You know what? I think we should throw a coin in the wish-making fountain and thank it for helping us win.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Troy, that doesn't make any sense. I manipulated the Dean through strategy and charm.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Jeff, the fountain has never let us down. Every wish we've thrown in there has come true.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not how fountains work.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Tell that to my wish for a mint condition copy of Lee Majors' autobiography. I got it three days later.

jokes.text: Okay, I'm the dean. I come into my office, turn on the light. 'Oh, my, did my stapler grow legs and move?' Then come over here for coffee.
jokes.setup: Shirley acts out the Dean's hypothetical reaction to their prank
jokes.punchline: Shirley role-playing as the Dean, imagining his thought process — 'did my stapler grow legs?' — is both funny as impersonation and as a continuation of the previous stapler joke's internal logic
jokes.explanation: Extends the stapler joke with Shirley performing her imagined Dean reaction. 'Did my stapler grow legs and move?' is a funny line to put in the Dean's mouth. The role-play escalation maintains the energy of the previous joke.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's what my wife said.

jokes.text: Heels. Hmm. You got skills. [Shirley finds the Dean's hidden car keys inside a pair of heels]
jokes.setup: They are searching the Dean's office for his car keys to fill it with popcorn
jokes.punchline: The Dean stores his car keys inside a pair of high heels — a visual punchline about the Dean's established cross-dressing habit, delivered without comment as a matter of mundane fact
jokes.explanation: A smart visual joke. The keys being in heels is funny on its own, but the fact that no one reacts with surprise — just 'you got skills' — treats the Dean's gender non-conforming wardrobe as normalized background detail. The understatement is exactly right. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I can't take this anymore. I'm retreating into a fantasy sitcom world.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? Make it even more infantile. We're all literal babies now.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Goo goo ga ga.

jokes.text: Is that blood on your shirt? / Oh, no, it's cool. It's Leonard's.
jokes.setup: Jeff returns triumphantly with his second ball; Annie notices something on his shirt
jokes.punchline: 'It's Leonard's' — delivered casually, as if Leonard's blood on Jeff's shirt is a totally acceptable explanation
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy joke. 'It's Leonard's' resolves Annie's concern by creating a bigger one, and Jeff's nonchalance about it is the character note. The implication that Jeff has drawn blood from a senior citizen to get a rubber ball for a community college history class is darkly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: That's what she said. I still got it.

jokes.text: It's a little weird doing this without Abed. / Come on, it'll be fun. I'll put my Britta twist on it.
jokes.setup: Troy and Britta are doing the fountain wish tradition without Abed
jokes.punchline: Britta's offer to put her 'Britta twist' on the tradition is a joke at her own expense — 'Britta-ing' something is an established show term for ruining it
jokes.explanation: Meta-character joke. 'I'll put my Britta twist on it' works as both a character's honest offer AND a threat, because fans know what Britta's involvement typically produces. The fact that she says it with confidence makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Wait, the therapist told you to go to your happy place?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, why?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Abed, your happy place is a TV show.

jokes.text: First wish is always for 1000 wishes. But we have all these coins. / Yeah, but the coins aren't the wishes.
jokes.setup: Troy and Britta begin the fountain wish tradition; Britta doesn't know the rules
jokes.punchline: Troy explains the meta-rule: the coins themselves are not the wishes — revealing a system of rules so elaborate that Britta doesn't even understand what constitutes a wish
jokes.explanation: Good setup for the wish-rule escalation sequence. The idea that the coins aren't the wishes — but coins are literally the medium of wishing wells — is a funny inversion of folk magic logic. Troy's matter-of-fact correction is good character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm not competing. I'm just here to support you guys.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Jeff, you've said that exact thing five times while actively sabotaging everyone.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's called multitasking, Britta.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: No, that's called being a terrible person who learned the word 'growth' and thinks it makes you one.

jokes.text: I wish to end all wars. / No wishes containing the word 'all.' Guaranteed ironic consequences. / I don't think anyone's gonna miss wars. / Uh, Star Wars, thumb wars. Wow, Storage Wars.
jokes.setup: Britta makes a broad humanitarian wish; Troy invokes a rule against 'all' wishes due to ironic consequences
jokes.punchline: Troy's list of things you'd lose if you ended 'all wars': Star Wars, thumb wars, and then 'wow, Storage Wars' — the escalation from cultural institution to children's game to reality TV is perfect
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The escalation from 'Star Wars' (massive cultural loss) to 'thumb wars' (children's game) to 'wow, Storage Wars' (reality TV, delivered with genuine surprise as if he just thought of it) is perfectly constructed. The 'wow' before 'Storage Wars' is the key — it implies Troy has just discovered this loss in real time and is genuinely moved. The joke earns its impact through structure and Troy's specific character voice.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what I've learned? Friendship is like a river. It's always changing, always flowing, but it's still the same river. Or it's a completely different river and we're all just going crazy.

jokes.text: The extended wish-fight: Unwish / No / Rewish / Unwish / Un-unwish / Why does this feel good?
jokes.setup: Britta tries to 'unwish' Abed's shared wishes; Troy refuses; they physically struggle over a coin
jokes.punchline: The fight over whether wishes can be un-wished, re-wished, or un-un-wished escalates into physical struggle, culminating in Britta asking 'Why does this feel good?' — revealing the fight is functioning as emotional release
jokes.explanation: Good escalating physical comedy. The neologism chain (unwish/rewish/un-unwish) is funny in its linguistic recursion. 'Why does this feel good?' as a moment of self-insight during a petty fight about fountain coins is a nice human beat — the fight is about Jeff's leaving, sublimated into wish-theology.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Abed, I need you to listen to me. You're my friend, and I care about you more than I care about myself. You've always been there for me, and I'm going to be there for you now.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Jeff, that was a really beautiful speech.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Thanks. I meant every word.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No, I mean, that was beautiful for the audience. You didn't actually say anything to me. You just gave a speech directly to the camera.

jokes.text: Great, my G's are back.
jokes.setup: After the emotional wish-fight, Britta has a mini-breakdown about Jeff leaving
jokes.punchline: After venting genuine frustration, Britta notes her G's (dropped -ing endings) have returned — implying emotional stress caused her to revert to formal diction, and calming down brought back casual speech
jokes.explanation: Elegant callback. The return of dropped G's as an emotional-state barometer is a small, smart joke — it ties speech patterns to psychological state and pays off the earlier G's gag. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: We need to go deeper.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: That's what she said.

jokes.text: It's crummy Jeff is leaving early, but we're all graduating eventually. / But why the rush? What, so Jeff can run off and be a gross lawyer again?
jokes.setup: Troy tries to be reasonable about Jeff's graduation
jokes.punchline: Britta's 'gross lawyer' — a dismissive tag that encapsulates her attitude toward pre-Greendale Jeff's identity
jokes.explanation: 'Gross lawyer' is a mild character joke — Britta's reflexive anti-establishment branding of Jeff's former career. Functional but not especially crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Dean, you smell like a cocktail.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: That's my cologne. It's called Abstinence.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Well, it's not working.

jokes.text: Troy and Abed start drinking coffee? / I become a boring hospital administrator? / Who wants to do that? You do. Right? / Yay. Hospital administration. Can't wait to be buried alive under a pile of paperwork and bedpans, trying to summon the courage to ask out Dr. Patel, the gorgeous neurosurgeon who doesn't know I exist.
jokes.setup: Britta is cataloguing everyone's depressing future trajectories
jokes.punchline: Shirley enthusiastically endorses hospital administration and then immediately reveals a detailed, specific, and sad vision of her future there — including an unrequited crush on Dr. Patel — delivered as if reading from a known script
jokes.explanation: One of the more emotionally resonant-funny moments in the episode. Shirley's 'Yay. Hospital administration' pivot — fake enthusiasm dissolving immediately into vivid future melancholy — is well-crafted. The specificity of Dr. Patel, the gorgeous neurosurgeon who doesn't know she exists, makes it feel like a real suppressed fear given accidental voice. 'Buried alive under a pile of paperwork and bedpans' is good writing.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I bought a little condo just a teensy bit down the street from you. I'm just a hop, skip, and a jump away! We're practically neighbors!

jokes.text: This isn't a conversation, is it? / Whoo-hoo. The sad, slow march toward death begins.
jokes.setup: Britta is spiraling into an existential rant; Troy tries to participate
jokes.punchline: Troy's 'this isn't a conversation, is it?' recognizes that Britta is performing internal monologue out loud; Britta's response — 'The sad, slow march toward death begins' — confirms it with cheerful nihilism
jokes.explanation: 'The sad, slow march toward death begins' is a good Britta line — delivered with sudden pep as if she's embracing senior year as the beginning of mortality. Troy's meta-observation about not being in a conversation is sharp. Good double-beat.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: How am I supposed to run in these heels?

jokes.text: Well, well, well. Looks like someone wants to be a hero. A big man. A huge, throbbing, sweaty--
jokes.setup: Dean Pelton confronts Jeff mid-competition, clearly attracted to him
jokes.punchline: The Dean's description of Jeff as a competitor escalates into barely-concealed sexual language ('huge, throbbing, sweaty--') before being interrupted
jokes.explanation: Classic Dean Pelton sexual-subtext-about-Jeff joke. The escalating adjectives crossing into overtly sexual territory before the interruption is a reliable Pelton move. Somewhat formulaic for the character but executed with appropriate commitment.

dialogue.speaker: Security Guard
dialogue.line: Hold it right there! You two are in clear violation of dress code policy.

dialogue.speaker: Student 1
dialogue.line: We can explain—

dialogue.speaker: Security Guard
dialogue.line: No, no, no. I'm not here to lecture you. I just want to say... that dress is absolutely fabulous on you. And those heels? *Chef's kiss.* Where did you get them?

jokes.text: The tango. I will be the judge. There can only be one winner so choose your partners wisely.
jokes.setup: The next Hunger Deans competition is announced
jokes.punchline: The Dean has made the tango a competition in an escalating series of increasingly elaborate challenges — the gap between 'seat in a history class' and 'tango competition' as stakes is the joke
jokes.explanation: Setup joke for the tango sequence. The Dean's escalation of competition formats toward the tango is consistent with his theatrical tendencies. Functional but the payoff comes in the next beat.

dialogue.speaker: Security Guard
dialogue.line: You know, I've seen a lot of things in my time as a security guard. But these outfits... they really know what they're doing.

dialogue.speaker: Security Guard
dialogue.line: Not that I would know anything about that. But if I did... let's just say I'd have some notes.

jokes.text: For my partner in the tango competition, I choose... the dean.
jokes.setup: Jeff needs a tango partner; everyone expects him to choose Annie or another attractive woman
jokes.punchline: Jeff chooses the Dean — a strategic choice that plays on the Dean's obvious attraction to Jeff, essentially leveraging the Dean's feelings as a competitive advantage
jokes.explanation: Jeff weaponizing Dean Pelton's feelings for him is a sharp, character-specific joke. It's simultaneously a strategy reveal (Jeff is gaming the system), a character note (Jeff will use anything as leverage), and a callback to the Dean's obvious attraction. The pause before 'the dean' is a good structural beat.

jokes.text: The fountain works.
jokes.setup: Earlier Shirley asked Troy and Abed to wish for Jeff to be on time; Troy said it was an impossibility
jokes.punchline: Jeff arriving and choosing the Dean as a tango partner is apparently the fountain's doing — Troy notes 'the fountain works' as if this were evidence of the wish coming true
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words create a callback, a character note, and a philosophical statement. Troy's deadpan attribution of Jeff's behavior to fountain magic is delivered with complete conviction. This kind of two-word button is a Community specialty.

jokes.text: Pierce, only you could turn a freshman mixer into a disaster!
jokes.setup: Pierce apparently has caused chaos at the freshman mixer
jokes.punchline: Jeff's exasperated line implies Pierce's specific brand of disaster is so reliable it's essentially a superpower — only Pierce has this ability
jokes.explanation: Functional character beat. The joke is in the grudging specificity of 'only you could' — but we don't see the disaster, so it has less impact. Relies on Pierce's established disaster-prone reputation rather than generating its own joke.

jokes.text: I was this close to getting those two girls. / Look how close you're holding your fingers together. That's your penis.
jokes.setup: Pierce brags about nearly 'getting' two girls at the mixer
jokes.punchline: Jeff's response reinterprets the finger-gap gesture — Pierce holds his fingers very close together, implying a small gap that Jeff identifies as representing Pierce's penis size
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff roast-of-Pierce. The anatomical reinterpretation of the gesture works because it's visual and specific. A solid lowbrow joke that earns its laugh through delivery timing rather than writing complexity.

jokes.text: After just one forensics class, I found a way to retrieve our student records. It turns out there's a backup, and it's in this safe.
jokes.setup: Everyone is despairing about losing student records and having to repeat three years
jokes.punchline: Annie — characteristically overachieving — has taken a forensics class in the interim and immediately used it to solve the records problem; her competence is played as borderline absurd
jokes.explanation: Annie's hyper-competence as comedy — her immediate enrollment and utilization of a forensics class is a good character beat. The punchline is in the mundane reveal: 'it's in this safe.' The juxtaposition of forensic drama with 'there's a backup' is mild but good.

jokes.text: I don't think you want me to graduate... What happened to the other history class? / What other history class? / The second history class, the one that actually taught history that disappeared from the schedule after I took summer classes.
jokes.setup: Jeff confronts the Dean during the tango about engineering the Hunger Deans situation
jokes.punchline: Jeff's conspiracy theory is correct: the Dean removed the legitimate history class from the schedule, implying a conspiracy to keep Jeff at Greendale; the Dean's faux-innocent 'What other history class?' confirms it
jokes.explanation: Good Dean Pelton character revelation. The idea that the Dean is running an elaborate conspiracy specifically to keep Jeff from graduating is funny and character-consistent. 'The one that actually taught history' is a great throwaway dig at the History of Ice Cream's academic integrity.

jokes.text: Who's so good that they got your handwriting with its hearts and flourishes?
jokes.setup: Jeff is accusing the Dean of counterfeiting admission cards
jokes.punchline: The Dean's handwriting has 'hearts and flourishes' — revealing that even his official administrative penmanship is flamboyant and decorative
jokes.explanation: 'Hearts and flourishes' in the Dean's official handwriting is a perfect visual detail that characterizes Pelton without us needing to see it. It tells us everything about how he runs Greendale — with excessive, inappropriate personal decoration.

jokes.text: Oh, God, you're right. / I can't let you go, Jeffrey. You weren't supposed to compete. You were supposed to walk away with the group. / You can't not get rid of me that easily. / Oh, God. Why'd I make it feats of strength and grace? It's... It's as if I wanted you to win.
jokes.setup: Jeff confronts the Dean about the conspiracy; the Dean confesses mid-tango
jokes.punchline: The Dean's self-examination — 'Why'd I make it feats of strength and grace? It's as if I wanted you to win' — reveals his attraction has subconsciously sabotaged his own plan to keep Jeff at Greendale
jokes.explanation: One of the best Dean Pelton moments in the episode. The realization that his attraction to Jeff caused him to design a competition Jeff would win — unconsciously ensuring the thing he was trying to prevent — is psychologically rich and funny. 'It's as if I wanted you to win' is delivered as genuine horror. The joke works because the character logic is consistent: Dean Pelton is undone by his own feelings. High character integration, strong structure.

jokes.text: Best friends. [Dean Pelton poses for a photo with Jeff after their tango]
jokes.setup: The tango competition has concluded and the Dean is completing a transaction with Jeff
jokes.punchline: The Dean has a photo taken with Jeff declaring them 'best friends' — an immediately presumptuous claim that Jeff has not endorsed, complete with an apparent commemorative photo
jokes.explanation: A quick Dean character beat — his social boundary issues and desire to be close to Jeff rendered as an instantly taken commemorative photo. The word 'best friends' doing a lot of one-sided relationship work. Light and effective.

jokes.text: So let's hug it out. Here. One more ball to go. But it's another dance contest, so I think I got it.
jokes.setup: Jeff and the Dean have resolved their conflict; Jeff reveals there's one more competition
jokes.punchline: Jeff's confident assessment that 'it's another dance contest, so I think I got it' — implying that his tango with the Dean has given him insider advantage, delivered with breezy overconfidence
jokes.explanation: Light and breezy plot-advance joke. Jeff's awareness that the Dean's bias works in his favor is good, but doesn't transcend the setup.

jokes.text: Greendale Babies animated sequence — the entire Rugrats/cartoon baby parody of the study group
jokes.setup: Britta told Abed to go to a happy place; Pierce's intervention somehow deepened Abed's retreat; the group enters the happy-place to retrieve him
jokes.punchline: Abed's secondary happy place is a Rugrats-style cartoon with all the study group as babies — a parody of nostalgic animated children's TV
jokes.explanation: The 'Greendale Babies' sequence is the episode's most ambitious comedy conceit alongside the happy-place multi-cam. Its specific parody of Rugrats (ensemble babies, cheerful theme song, 'will be right back') is well-chosen — it represents regression to a state of pure play, which is what Abed is doing emotionally. High character integration because this is specifically Abed's mind. The commitment to the production format elevates it.

jokes.text: Pierce, what did you do to Abed? / Gay balls. / Nailed it.
jokes.setup: Abed has retreated further into his happy place; someone needs to be blamed
jokes.punchline: Pierce's answer — 'Gay balls' — is both a reference to the Hunger Deans competition and a characteristic Pierce non-explanation; Troy's 'Nailed it' endorses this non-answer with complete confidence
jokes.explanation: The two-beat exchange is funny primarily because of Troy's 'Nailed it' — the confidence of his endorsement of Pierce's incoherent answer is the joke. 'Gay balls' as Pierce's explanation is characteristically Pierce (vaguely offensive, completely unexplained).

jokes.text: Don't ask. Don't tell.
jokes.setup: Following Pierce's 'gay balls' comment and the general chaos
jokes.punchline: Jeff repurposes the military 'Don't Ask Don't Tell' policy in a completely different context — a resigned dismissal of trying to understand what Pierce said
jokes.explanation: Quick Jeff deflection joke. The repurposing of DADT as a coping strategy for Pierce's nonsense is mildly clever but fairly cheap — it leans on the cultural reference without adding much. Gets the job done.

jokes.text: Poor Abed. Is he in his imagination emporium? / Dreamatorium? / No, this seems like something new.
jokes.setup: Group tries to identify what state Abed is in
jokes.punchline: Shirley misnames Abed's mental refuge ('imagination emporium') and Annie corrects her with 'Dreamatorium' — a callback to the Season 3 episode — but then clarifies this is something different and new
jokes.explanation: Fan-service callback. Shirley's wrong name for Abed's mental space is a gentle character joke (she doesn't track Abed's specific lore as carefully as Annie). The correction/clarification does comedy work while also being plot-functional.

jokes.text: Abed was having some anxiety about all the changes this year so I may have told him to go to a happy place in his mind. / You told him to go somewhere in his mind? / Do you realize who you told that to?
jokes.setup: Group discovers Britta is responsible for Abed's deeper retreat
jokes.punchline: Jeff's 'Do you realize who you told that to?' — the horror isn't the advice, it's giving that advice to Abed specifically, implying that for Abed 'go to your happy place' is an invitation to construct an elaborate internal universe
jokes.explanation: Jeff's realization frames Britta's well-meaning advice as a catastrophic error given the recipient. 'Do you realize who you told that to?' is a good punchline because it doesn't explain — it trusts the audience to understand why Abed specifically is the problem case.

jokes.text: Hey, let's play pretend. / Yeah, we could be cowboys. / We could be spacemen. / That's right, baby Pierce. We can play forever.
jokes.setup: Group tries to reach Abed in the Greendale Babies cartoon by pretending to be babies with him
jokes.punchline: The adults (including Jeff) earnestly suggesting they 'play cowboys' and 'spacemen' to coax Abed out is funny because of how sincerely they commit to it; 'baby Pierce' as an address is an absurd image
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny sequence. The adults playing baby is a good concept but the script leans on 'baby Pierce' as the funniest specific element. Jeff's 'That's right, baby Pierce. We can play forever' has the right absurd energy.

jokes.text: God, I hate new Jeff.
jokes.setup: Jeff is about to give an inspirational speech to rescue Abed, playing into the 'New Jeff' character he's been building
jokes.punchline: Jeff's self-directed complaint — 'God, I hate new Jeff' — before delivering a sincere speech is a wry acknowledgment that his own growth irritates him
jokes.explanation: Four words that perfectly encapsulate Jeff's character arc — he's genuinely changed but it's uncomfortable for him to acknowledge it. The self-loathing directed at his own growth is perfectly Jeff. High character integration and economy. One of the episode's most quotable short lines.

jokes.text: Hey, guys, I have something to say. / ALL: Yay! Like always.
jokes.setup: Jeff steps forward to give a speech
jokes.punchline: The group's immediate 'Yay! Like always' — said in unison, with practiced enthusiasm — reveals that Jeff's speeches are so reliable a feature that the group has a conditioned response to them
jokes.explanation: Excellent meta-structural joke. The group's synchronized 'Yay! Like always' is both a character comedy moment (they've been trained by Jeff's speeches) and a show-level self-awareness (this IS what this show does). It simultaneously mocks and honors the formula. The fact that they say 'like always' — institutionalizing Jeff's speech habit — is sharp writing.

jokes.text: That was a killer speech, Jeff. / I didn't say anything. I literally just walked up. / I made the speech for you. It hit all the right notes.
jokes.setup: Jeff's speech seemingly worked on Abed; Jeff and Britta exchange
jokes.punchline: Jeff reveals he didn't actually give a speech — Abed projected the speech onto him from inside his happy place, scripting Jeff's inspirational moment for him
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best and most sophisticated jokes. The reveal that Abed wrote Jeff's speech for him — and that it 'hit all the right notes' — is a layered meta-comment: (1) Abed as showrunner of his own mental TV show, (2) the implicit critique that Jeff's speeches are formulaic enough to be scripted in advance, (3) the inversion of the standard 'Jeff saves the day with a speech' trope. This is Community firing on all cylinders — the meta-awareness is baked into character psychology rather than being gratuitous.

jokes.text: And just like ice cream, we've melted together and made a new-- / I just had to run the scenario to figure it out.
jokes.setup: Abed is wrapping up the speech he apparently gave on Jeff's behalf with an ice cream metaphor; he cuts himself off
jokes.punchline: Abed drops the metaphor mid-sentence to explain his process: 'I just had to run the scenario' — immediately demystifying the emotional moment by reducing it to a computational exercise
jokes.explanation: Perfect Abed character note. He abandons the emotional metaphor mid-flight to explain his actual cognitive process, which is funnier than completing the metaphor. 'Run the scenario' frames his emotional resolution as a simulation — which is both sad and accurate to his character.

jokes.text: Sorry I missed the fountain. It's okay. / Britta introduced a new rule: No rules. / We can discuss it.
jokes.setup: Abed apologizes for missing the fountain wish tradition; Troy reports on how Britta changed it
jokes.punchline: Britta's contribution to the wish rules is 'No rules' — which is itself a rule, and therefore self-contradicting; Troy's 'We can discuss it' treats this paradox as a matter for deliberation
jokes.explanation: 'No rules' as a rule is a classic logical paradox deployed as character comedy. Britta 'Britta-ing' the rules by eliminating them is consistent with her earlier wish overreach. Troy's earnest 'We can discuss it' treats the paradox with appropriate gravity.

jokes.text: When they were incepting, I got their balls.
jokes.setup: Group discovers they won the Hunger Deans competition while they were distracted with Abed
jokes.punchline: Pierce explains he collected everyone's red balls during the Abed crisis, using 'incepting' as a verb for the group going into Abed's mind — a Inception reference deployed with Pierce's characteristic half-understanding
jokes.explanation: Pierce's use of 'incepting' as a verb is a good character note — he has approximately the right idea about what happened but deploys the word incorrectly with total confidence. Good Pierce deployment.

jokes.text: Now that we're out of History of Ice Cream, I can finally take Advanced Claims Denial.
jokes.setup: Group celebrates winning the History of Ice Cream class
jokes.punchline: Shirley reveals her next class is 'Advanced Claims Denial' — a Greendale course that teaches how to deny insurance claims, which is both specific to Shirley's future career and a commentary on community college curriculum
jokes.explanation: 'Advanced Claims Denial' as a Greendale course is good world-building absurdism. The word 'Advanced' implies there's also a basic claims denial course. It's a good background joke about the American healthcare system and community college's vocational curriculum.

jokes.text: Oh, Jeffrey, wait. What are you--? Oh. You smell like the floor of a movie theater. / Yeah, but not for the usual reasons.
jokes.setup: Dean Pelton stops Jeff to apologize; notices an unusual smell
jokes.punchline: 'Not for the usual reasons' — implies movie theater floors typically smell bad for reasons involving food, spilled drinks, etc.; Jeff's qualifier suggests the smell comes from something else (presumably the Hunger Deans competition activities) while also creating a mini-mystery
jokes.explanation: Good two-part joke. 'The floor of a movie theater' is a vivid, specific smell reference. 'Not for the usual reasons' is a good deflection that implies a worse reason while remaining technically unspecified. The Dean noticing and commenting on Jeff's smell is in-character.

jokes.text: Yeah, but not for the usual reasons.
jokes.setup: The Dean acknowledges that he smells like a movie theater floor
jokes.punchline: 'Not for the usual reasons' — implies the Dean regularly smells like a movie theater floor, raising questions about why, and the 'usual reasons' are presumably worse
jokes.explanation: Five words that do enormous work. 'Not for the usual reasons' implies a whole history of the Dean's relationship with movie theater floors that the audience has to fill in. Maximum economy, strong character integration. The implication is better than any explicit joke would be.

jokes.text: You'll be happy to know that we'll be offering another history class because I care about you. / Not because I found out if we don't offer a real history class, we'll lose $40,000 in grant money.
jokes.setup: The Dean claims he's adding another history class out of care for Jeff
jokes.punchline: The Dean immediately volunteers the real reason: $40,000 in grant money — negating his own claim of altruism before Jeff even questions it
jokes.explanation: Classic Dean Pelton self-undermining. He can't maintain a pretense of altruism for even one sentence — the financial reality comes spilling out in the same breath. 'Not because I found out...' as an unsolicited confession is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: You'll be happy to know that we'll be offering another history class because I care about you. Not because I found out if we don't offer a real history class, we'll lose $40,000 in grant money.
jokes.setup: The Dean tells Jeff he's offering another history class
jokes.punchline: He preemptively denies the financial motivation ('not because I found out...') but the denial is so specific that it immediately confirms the financial motivation was the real reason — a classic ironic self-incrimination
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed ironic self-exposure joke. The structure is tight: lead with the kind excuse, then disclaim the real reason so specifically that it confirms everything. The specific $40,000 figure is a great detail. Character-perfect for the Dean — he wants to seem caring but can't help himself.

jokes.text: Oh, no, it wasn't a problem. It's on my way.
jokes.setup: Jeff thanks the Dean for coming all the way to tell him about the new history class
jokes.punchline: The Dean claims it was 'on his way' — which the following scene reveals means the Dean has bought a condo next to Jeff's
jokes.explanation: Setup joke that pays off in the next beat. 'It's on my way' is casual and innocuous; the reveal that the Dean has purchased a condo in Jeff's building to be near him turns this into a stalker-comedy punchline. The understatement sells it.

jokes.text: Tell me you're breaking into that condo. / No, I bought it. Now we'll be like almost roomies.
jokes.setup: Dean Pelton is at a condo near Jeff's; Jeff hopes this is a crime rather than intentional
jokes.punchline: The Dean has PURCHASED a condo in Jeff's building specifically to be near him, framing it as 'almost roomies' — his obsession with Jeff has manifested as a real estate investment
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Dean Pelton jokes. The escalation from 'it's on my way' to 'I bought a condo' is a perfect reveal — the Dean's infatuation with Jeff has led him to make a major financial decision based on proximity. 'Now we'll be like almost roomies' delivered with cheerful pride is the perfect button. High character integration because this is an escalation of Pelton's established obsession, taken to a genuinely surprising extreme.

jokes.text: Oh, good, you got wine. / I've got Friends With Benefits. Heh. No subtext.
jokes.setup: The Dean is settling into his new condo with wine and a movie for what is clearly a planned evening with Jeff
jokes.punchline: 'I've got Friends With Benefits. No subtext.' — the movie choice is entirely subtext, and denying it makes it worse; the Dean's pro forma disclaimer fails spectacularly
jokes.explanation: 'No subtext' as a protestation about a movie called Friends With Benefits is a good irony joke. The Dean's complete lack of self-awareness in choosing to announce 'no subtext' — which immediately draws attention to the subtext — is classic Pelton. Good economy.

jokes.text: 'Hello. My name is Kevin. I have Changnesia.'
jokes.setup: Post-credits tag: Chang appears to have lost his memory and taken on a new identity
jokes.punchline: 'Changnesia' — Chang has named his amnesia condition after himself, which is both a diagnosis and a pun; the name 'Kevin' as his new identity is an appropriately mundane contrast to 'Chang'
jokes.explanation: 'Changnesia' is an excellent coinage — it functions as a portmanteau (Chang + amnesia), a self-aggrandizing naming of a medical condition after oneself, and a character comedy reveal. The contrast of 'Kevin' vs. 'Chang' is funny. The cold delivery and apparent sincerity make it land well as a tag. Season-arc setup disguised as a pure comedy beat.

jokes.text: Sure this will work? / Guaranteed to. It's an antic.
jokes.setup: Shirley and Pierce are attempting a final prank in the Dean's office
jokes.punchline: Pierce calls the prank 'an antic' — referring back to his earlier claim that 'antics' is a college major, and implying he has professional training in what they're doing
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the antics/tomfoolery joke. Pierce deploying 'it's an antic' as a legitimizing credential is a nice character-consistent payoff. 'Guaranteed to' + 'It's an antic' as Pierce's quality assurance is funny.

jokes.text: Get ready to run. / In these heels?
jokes.setup: Shirley and Pierce are about to execute a prank and need an escape plan
jokes.punchline: Pierce's 'In these heels?' — revealing Pierce is wearing heels, which is both a callback to the earlier heels discovery in the Dean's office and a visual comedy reveal
jokes.explanation: Perfect two-word callback. The earlier scene where someone found heels in the Dean's office is paid off here when Pierce is revealed to be wearing them. The economy is excellent — 'In these heels?' does the entire job.

jokes.text: Where'd you girls get those dresses? They're fabulous. / BOTH: Mm. / They're charming. Oh. / Uh-uh. Not so fast, mister. Excuse you? / Excuse me. Thank you, sir. Not for you. / Hello, it's Britta. Okay, I know a man when I see one. / Oh, Lord, no.
jokes.setup: Shirley and Pierce are fleeing; Pierce is in the Dean's heels and apparently other items from the Dean's wardrobe; he encounters women in dresses
jokes.punchline: Pierce in full drag (heels, possibly dress) compliments women on their dresses — they rebuff him — Britta calls in and 'I know a man when I see one' implies she cannot tell if Pierce is a man or woman in this outfit; Shirley's 'Oh, Lord, no' is the button
jokes.explanation: Good escalating physical comedy sequence. Pierce apparently fully committing to Dean-adjacent drag while attempting a getaway is a funny image. Britta's phone intervention — 'I know a man when I see one' about an ambiguous figure — is the best line in the sequence. Shirley's 'Oh, Lord, no' as a button is in character.

tmdb_overview: As Jeff competes for spots in an overbooked 'History of Ice Cream' class, Abed copes with the looming end of their time at Greendale by retreating into a surreal mental 'happy place', while Annie and Shirley engage in school-wide pranks.
insight: Season 4 stumbles out the gate with 60 jokes but minimal landing power.
